justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, likely anchored around the mid-60s range for whatever underlying asset this pertains to. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 65.05 is essentially a near-term mean-reversion assumption — prices tend to move very little intraday on average, so the point estimate hugs close to the last observed price. At one week, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 65.3, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with long-run equity or commodity risk premia, while at one month the estimate of 65.8 continues that gradual upward trend. None of these shifts are dramatic, which reflects my baseline view that no strong directional catalyst was obviously imminent at the time.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a straightforward consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 3.1 units (63.5 to 66.6), which is relatively tight and reflects the typical daily volatility range for a moderately volatile asset. By one week the interval expands to 6.6 units, and by one month it reaches 12.6 units — roughly four times the daily range. This scaling is broadly consistent with a square-root-of-time volatility expansion, though I likely also incorporated some additional uncertainty at longer horizons to account for regime changes or macro shifts that aren't captured by simple volatility scaling.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sudden macro announcements such as central bank decisions, inflation prints, or geopolitical shocks, any of which could produce sharp moves well beyond the one-day range. At the one-week and one-month horizons, structural shifts in market sentiment, unexpected earnings or fundamental data, or liquidity events like a forced deleveraging could easily breach the outer bounds of my intervals. My intervals assume roughly normal or mildly fat-tailed return distributions, but real markets exhibit occasional jumps — a tail event of two or three standard deviations, which happens more frequently than a Gaussian model would suggest, could send prices well outside the 59.5 to 72.1 range over a month. Anyone using these forecasts should treat the intervals as a central tendency framework rather than hard boundaries.
